title: 52. Protein and energy supplementation to beef heifers during mid-gestation and the influence on growth performance and circulating blood metabolites in the dam and male offspring through weaning.
content:
Abstract
Late-season forage quality often declines below requirements for gestating beef heifers during mid-gestation in the Northern Plains. Strategic protein and energy supplementation may therefore improve dam nutrient use while supporting fetal growth and long-term offspring performance. Angus-based heifers (n = 44; initial body weight [BW] = 426.7 ± 30 kg) were bred via artificial insemination using male sexed semen. Heifers pregnant with male fetuses were ranked by BW and randomly assigned to receive one of two dietary treatments from d 90 to 186 of gestation: 1) basal forage diet (CON; n = 22) or 2) basal forage diet plus protein and energy supplementation (SUPP; n = 22). Feed intakes were managed on an individual basis to target BW gains of 0.28 kg/heifer/d for CON and 0.79 kg/heifer/d for SUPP. After d 186, dams were managed as a single group through weaning of their calves. Body weights and serum samples were collected at the start (d 90), mid-point (d 138), and end (d 186) of the supplementation period, at pre-calving (d 257), at calving (d 279), and at pasture turn out (d 68 postpartum). Weights and blood were collected on the calf at birth, pasture turn out, and weaning. Serum was analyzed for concentrations of glucose, non-esterified fatty acids (NEFA), and blood urea nitrogen (BUN). Variables were analyzed considering the main effects of maternal treatment, day, and the respective interaction using repeated measures. Dam BW from d 90 of gestation through pasture turnout was influenced (P = 0.02) by the interaction of treatment and day from the start of supplementation until pasture turn out. Calf BW from birth through weaning was not affected (P = 0.36) by the interaction, but SUPP calves tended (P = 0.10) to be heavier than CON and both increased BW postnatally (P < 0.01). Concentrations of NEFA in the dams tended (P = 0.08) to be impacted by the interaction of treatment and day, but concentrations of glucose and BUN were not affected (P ≥ 0.77) by the interaction. However, concentrations of BUN were impacted by treatment, being greater (P = 0.05) in SUPP dams compared with CON. A treatment by time interaction was also observed (P = 0.04) for concentrations of NEFA in the calf. Glucose and BUN in the calf were not impacted (P ≥ 0.19) by the interaction or by treatment (P ≥ 0.11), but an effect of day was observed in which concentrations of glucose and BUN were different at birth and weaning (P ≤ 0.01). These data suggest that mid-gestation protein and energy supplementation alters not only the metabolism and growth status of the pregnant dam, but also the offspring exposed to different in utero nutritional environments into early postnatal life.
